claims.text: The initial material is a quaternary equiatomic FCC alloy with a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
The alloy contains SRO clusters approximately 1.2 nm in size.
SRO clusters act as pinning points for edge dislocations.
Yield strength will become insensitive to strain rate between 300 K and 500 K.
Strain-rate insensitivity is caused by saturation of SRO pinning forces.
An approximately 1.2 nm SRO length scale becomes the dominant barrier to dislocation motion.
Dominance of the SRO barrier renders dislocation glide independent of thermal-activation rates.
A phase-transformation deformation mechanism would remain strongly strain-rate sensitive.
The proposed intervention is uniaxial tension over strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1 and temperatures from 300 K to 600 K.
Mechanical testing is to be conducted without irradiation or corrosive media.
Dislocation glide initially requires thermal activation to overcome SRO pinning barriers.
At intermediate temperatures, the rate-limiting process shifts from thermally activated barrier crossing to athermal dislocation bowing.
The shift to athermal dislocation bowing causes yield strength to plateau with respect to strain rate.
A phase-transformation mechanism would produce a continuous decrease in yield strength with increasing temperature.
Standard FCC dislocation-glide behavior involves decreasing yield strength with temperature and increasing yield strength with strain rate.
The proposed behavior applies only when SRO is the dominant microstructural feature.
Precipitates such as Laves or Heusler phases would invalidate the proposed SRO-dominated behavior.
Temperatures above the SRO ordering temperature would dissolve SRO and invalidate the hypothesis.
The specific SRO-dislocation interaction and its characteristic influence length are not fully characterized.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if yield strength depends significantly on strain rate at 400 K or if an FCC-to-HCP transformation initiates at yielding.
